I spent the summer of 2026 as a trainee in financial advisory, modelling client plans and analysing a six-fund portfolio. Since September I have been studying Financial Mathematics at Charles University, and in my first year I enrolled in a practitioner-led course on financial risk measurement and management.

tools.title: Tools
tools.heading: Three models I programmed in order to understand them.

items.title: Black–Scholes
items.summary: European option, no dividends, constant volatility σ.
items.quote: I built an option pricer to understand what risk managers look at, not to rediscover the formula.

ui.aria: Chart of option value against the underlying price with the payoff at expiry and the current price marked
ui.live: Option price {price}, delta {delta}, theta {theta} per day.

details: C = S·N(d₁) − K·e^(−rT)·N(d₂); P = K·e^(−rT)·N(−d₂) − S·N(−d₁)
N(x) is computed through erf (Abramowitz–Stegun 7.1.26, error below 1.5·10⁻⁷).
Δ = N(d₁) for a call, N(d₁) − 1 for a put; Γ = φ(d₁)/(S·σ·√T); ν = S·φ(d₁)·√T / 100 (per 1 pp of σ); Θ per day = Θ per year / 365.
Assumptions: European exercise, no dividends, constant σ and r, continuous compounding.
items.insight: Theta accelerates as expiry approaches: an at-the-money option loses value fastest in its final weeks. Shorten T and watch the curve collapse onto the payoff.

items.title: Monte Carlo
items.summary: Geometric Brownian motion with daily steps, jumps following Merton's crash model.
items.quote: I built it to get a feel for modelling uncertainty. What surprised me most was how badly the normal model underestimates crash risk.

ui.aria: Chart of simulated price paths with the median, percentiles and the 5% VaR level; a histogram of terminal values on the right
ui.live: Median terminal price {median}, 5% VaR {var}, expected shortfall {es}, probability of loss {ploss}.

details: Sₜ₊Δₜ = Sₜ · exp[(μ − σ²/2)·Δt + σ·√Δt · z], Δt = 1/252 (daily step), z ~ N(0, 1) via Box–Muller.

Jump model (Merton 1976): with probability λ·Δt per day a jump exp(J) arrives, J ~ N(−0.15, 0.10²), λ = 0.5 per year; the drift is compensated by λ·κ·Δt (κ = e^(μ_J + σ_J²/2) − 1) so the expected price stays the same.
5% VaR = S₀ − 5th percentile of terminal values; 5% ES = S₀ − mean of the worst 5% of terminal values; P(loss) = share of paths with Sₜ < S₀.
Both models are always computed from the same seed so the columns can be compared; the chart shows the selected model.
Note: Student-t innovations on daily steps average out over longer horizons (CLT) and the terminal distribution approaches the normal one, which is why crashes are modelled as jumps.
items.insight: Same drift and volatility, plus only rare downward jumps (one every two years on average, typically around −14%). The median barely moves, but the 5% VaR and the expected shortfall grow substantially. The normal model would call such a drop practically impossible; the paths below its VaR level are drawn in oxide red.

items.title: Markowitz
items.summary: Single-period model with three assets and no transaction costs.
items.quote: I programmed the efficient frontier to understand why diversification works, and above all where the model breaks down.

ui.caption: This is how sensitive the frontier is to the input estimates.
ui.aria: Scatter chart of portfolios in the risk and return plane with the efficient frontier, the minimum-variance portfolio and the maximum-Sharpe portfolio
ui.psdNote: The correlations entered are mutually inconsistent or nearly singular, so they are scaled towards zero by a factor of {c}.
ui.noTangency: No portfolio beats the risk-free rate, so there is no tangency portfolio.

details: E[r_p] = Σ wᵢ·μᵢ; σ_p² = Σᵢ Σⱼ wᵢ·wⱼ·ρᵢⱼ·σᵢ·σⱼ; Sharpe = (E[r_p] − r_f) / σ_p; Σ wᵢ = 1, without shorting wᵢ ≥ 0.
Frontier = upper envelope of 3,000 random portfolios (no shorting: weights from normalised |N(0,1)|; with shorting: from N(0,1) limited to [−1, 2]) plus the two-asset mixes.
Estimation error: 20 scenarios with μᵢ ± 1.5 pp and σᵢ ± 10% (fixed seed); their frontiers are drawn and the half-range of the max-Sharpe weights is reported as ±.

The three correlations entered must form a positive definite matrix; I require its smallest eigenvalue to be at least 0.05. If it is not, all three are scaled towards zero by the same factor until it is, and a note appears under the chart.
Assumptions: one period, no transaction costs; the inputs are themselves estimates.
items.insight: The model is sensitive to its inputs: shifting expected returns by 1–2 percentage points reshuffles the "optimal" portfolio substantially. That is why raw Markowitz is rarely used on its own in practice; constraints, shrinkage estimators or Black–Litterman views are layered on top.
